newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian Liburnia sees losses shrinking in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Croatian Liburnia sees losses shrinking in 1997.

text.p: Croatia's state-owned hotelier Liburnia-Riviera said on Monday it hoped losses accumulated during war years will be minimised in 1997 with an increase in business and slightly higher prices.

"Our plans were very modest with a 10 percent increase in overnights and 12 percent in income to 157 million kuna ($25.8 million). But we'll still have a minor loss this year," chief executive Nikola Slavic told Reuters in an interview.
He said all signs so far pointed to a slightly better performance than was planned, but underlying problems made it unlikely that Liburnia-Riviera would break even just yet.
The group, comprising some 20 hotels and holiday villas with 4,368 beds in and around Croatia's oldest Adriatic seaside resort, ended 1996 with a 56 million kuna net loss.
Slavic put the operating loss at around 20 million, mostly because the facilities accommodated some 1,200 refugees for which the company was poorly compensated by the government.
It also lost money on the sale of one of the hotels to settle an old debt and made a 16-17 million kuna provision against depreciation of assets.
"The refurbishment of existing facilities is vital," Slavic said, adding Liburnia-Riviera was making hurried preparations to revamp the stylish three-star Hotel Belvedere.
A 20 million German mark ($11.6 million) joint venture with an Italian investor, including turning the Belvedere's attached Villa Rosalia into a casino, is expected to start in September.
"Being short of capital, we see our future in joint ventures and there are a lot of interested parties," Slavic said.
All projects have to be put to international tender and approved by the government which controls more than 90 percent of the group via its privatisation agency and pension funds.
Of 302.6 million marks equity, some 96 million are reserved for pre-World War Two owners and current and former employees bought 8.2 percent when the group was put up for privatisation six years ago.
The group has managed to win back some clients from richer Western European countries who only visited Croatia in small numbers during the war in former Yugoslavia.
Germans, Austrians, Britons, Italians and the Dutch in pre-1991 years traditionally outstripped Croatian holiday makers in the pricey resort of Opatija.

Now the number of tourists from former communist countries is seen falling after the price increase, but Slavic said they were not great spenders for anything except bed and board. ($ = 6.096 Croatian Kuna) ($ = 1.723 German Marks)
